transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yes, it's nice to meet you too. Um, well, I came in because things at the lab are just... it's my work. I'm a physical scientist, and lately I just absolutely cannot keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. It's becoming this massive, catastrophic problem for my team. 

Like, we will be in the middle of a really crucial grant call—you know, where our funding for the next two years is completely on the line and I need to be answering questions from the committee—or even just a mandatory safety meeting, and I'll just... I'll notice something else. It could be anything. I'll hear this faint pump vibration down the hall and realize the frequency is off by a fraction of a hertz, or one of my undergrad students will make some completely offhand side comment about a completely different project, or my brain will just suddenly flash to some odd peak in an old spectrum from a sample we ran three years ago that we never fully resolved. 

And instead of focusing on the grant, or the safety protocols, or whatever it is I am strictly supposed to be doing, suddenly I'm just... I'm off chasing that new thing. For hours and hours. I'll leave the meeting, or mute the call, and go physically dismantle the vacuum pump, or I'll pull up gigabytes of old spectral data and start cross-referencing it with literature from the nineties, and I just get so completely absorbed in it that I lose all track of time. And meanwhile, the actual thing everyone needs from me—the primary experiment, the approvals, the funding—it just completely falls apart. My colleagues are furious, the administration is sending me emails, and I try to explain to them how important that spectral peak was, but they just look at me like I'm crazy because I completely derailed a federal grant call over it. I just can't seem to filter anything out anymore, everything feels equally urgent, and I just keep going down these massive rabbit holes while my actual career is just sitting there burning to the ground...
Have you been needing much less sleep than usual and still feeling full of energy?

Yes, actually, that's exactly it. It's... it's honestly like sleep has just become this incredibly inefficient interruption to everything I need to get done. Most nights lately, I'm only sleeping maybe two or three hours total. And I don't even make it to my actual bedroom anymore. I'll just be sitting on the living room couch, because I brought my laptop out there to run a quick baseline analysis on those old spectral files I was telling you about, and I'll just sort of briefly pass out right there with the laptop still open and running on my lap. 

But the crazy thing is, when I wake up at, say, 3:30 or 4:00 in the morning, I don't feel groggy at all. Not even a little bit. I don't need coffee, I don't need to rub my eyes or try to wake up. I just open my eyes and my brain is instantly firing. I am completely sharp, totally energized, and just immediately ready to dive back into the work. I mean, why spend eight hours unconscious when I have gigabytes of data to sort through and I feel this awake? It just feels like a biological design flaw to sleep when I have all this energy. My colleagues are complaining about being exhausted after a normal shift, and I'm running on two hours feeling like I could power the entire lab facility myself. There's just too much to do, and I just don't seem to need the rest right now.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don’t seem to?

No, no, I haven't experienced anything like that. I mean, my brain is definitely moving a million miles a minute, and I'm processing all this data and noticing all these tiny details—like the pump vibration I mentioned, or the way a specific colleague will sigh right before they ask a question about the budget—but it's all real things. It's all actually there. I'm just picking up on it more acutely than anyone else is right now. 

I'm not, you know, hallucinating or seeing ghosts in the lab or hearing voices telling me what to do with the spectral data. It's just my own thoughts, my own voice in my head, just... moving very, very fast. And the things I see are just the actual readouts, the actual emails, the actual equipment. I might be hyper-focused on them, and maybe I'm connecting dots that other people aren't seeing yet because they're too bogged down in the mundane administrative stuff, but the dots themselves are completely real. So, no, nothing like that. I'm just... I'm just incredibly tuned in to the actual physical environment around me right now. Probably more tuned in than I've ever been in my entire career, honestly.
